slides.title: Agentic AI for Utility Operators
slides.say: Welcome. I am Alaa Selim, from MIT/Dartmouth, presenting with Mohamed Chehada from UT Austin. Our question is how an AI agent can help a power engineer or operator complete a useful, checkable task. We will define the basic ideas, examine industry reports, work through power-system research and learn how to judge the evidence. Two short exercises will let you make the checks yourself. The separate hands-on tutorial then applies these ideas to voltage support, restoration and cyber response.
slides.visual: Introduce the presenters and the session route. Ask learners to keep one task from their own work in mind throughout the session.
slides.question: Which task would you like an assistant to help you complete?
slides.answer: Accept a specific task such as checking study inputs, locating event records or reviewing an outage. Reuse one audience example later.
slides.transition: First, what do we mean by agentic AI?

slides.title: What is agentic AI?
slides.say: We use agentic AI to describe a system that works toward a goal, reads the results of its actions and adjusts its next step. One agent can do this. Imagine asking whether a previous voltage study still applies after a switch changes position. The system may inspect the event, identify the study case, run an allowed check and ask for missing evidence. The important question is who chooses those steps and what feedback changes the choice. Definitions vary across the literature. Anthropic uses agentic systems to include both programmed workflows and model-directed agents. We will keep that source's terminology explicit rather than present one universal definition.
slides.visual: Trace each NVIDIA interaction pattern from the request through the model to tools or other agents. Point out that the same model can appear in more than one arrangement. The figure illustrates patterns rather than a required hierarchy.
slides.question: Does an agentic system need several agents?
slides.answer: No. A single agent with appropriate feedback and tools can carry out a bounded task.
slides.transition: We should first separate content generation from choosing actions.

slides.title: Generative AI creates content
slides.say: Generative AI produces content such as text, images or audio. A large language model, or LLM, handles language. In our report example, selected records and a request enter the model and a draft comes out. That can be useful on its own. An agent system can use the same model repeatedly to decide which evidence to request next. These ideas overlap. They describe roles within a system, rather than three technologies that replace one another. A clear paragraph about voltage also needs a traceable numerical result behind it. Fluent wording tells us how readable a report is. Engineering evidence tells us whether the conclusion follows from the study.
slides.visual: Follow the diagram from records and request to the model and draft. Identify the engineering records as inputs. Ask where a numerical claim in the draft could be checked.
slides.question: If a model writes a good study summary, has it necessarily acted as an agent?
slides.answer: No. A single generation call may create the summary. We need to inspect the surrounding process to identify decision making and tool use.
slides.transition: The classical definition of an agent helps us identify that process.

slides.title: What is an AI agent?
slides.say: An AI agent observes an environment and chooses actions that affect it. This definition predates large language models. In the textbook picture, observations arrive through sensors and actions leave through actuators. For a software study assistant, the observations may be case files, measurements and solver logs. Its actions may be requests to a database or a simulator. The decision rule uses what has been observed so far. That does not require a robot or a physical actuator. It also does not require unrestricted autonomy. We choose the task and permissions. A solver can remain responsible for electrical calculations while an agent decides which permitted study to request next.
slides.visual: Start with the environment, follow the sensor arrow into the agent, then the actuator arrow back out. Translate each element into a software study example. The source figure is an older author-hosted textbook chapter.
slides.question: What could count as an observation for a grid-study agent?
slides.answer: A versioned case file, a timestamped measurement, a solver status or a returned constraint violation.
slides.transition: Now separate the part that chooses an action from the part that carries it out.

slides.title: An agent chooses a step. A tool runs it.
slides.say: The agent chooses a permitted step. A tool performs a defined operation and returns a result. For example, the agent can request a power-flow calculation for case F12. The tool interface should identify the case, input versions and settings. The solver then calculates the voltages and flows. The returned evidence should include status and a record that can be inspected. If the solver reports an error, the agent may choose another allowed check or ask for help. The surrounding runtime executes the calls and saves progress. Planning and memory can support that process, although every design need not use separate modules for them. The architecture alone gives no authority to operate equipment.
slides.visual: Point from the core to tools, then back to the returned result. Identify planning and memory as possible supporting roles. Use the run_pf case example rather than interpreting every box as a mandatory component.
slides.question: Who calculates the voltage in this example?
slides.answer: The engineering solver. The agent chooses the request and uses the solver's returned evidence.
slides.transition: A workflow can also call tools, so the next distinction concerns control of the sequence.

slides.title: Workflow or agent: who chooses the next step?
slides.say: In a fixed workflow, the code defines the steps and branches. For example, every case may pass through input validation, power flow and reporting. In an LLM agent, the model chooses some next steps from the allowed actions using the evidence so far. A design can combine both. We may require validation in code while allowing the model to choose which diagnostic tool to call. Anthropic's distinction is useful for engineering discussions, but it does not cover every historical meaning of agent. A loop alone is also insufficient evidence of model-directed choice. Inspect the actual routing rule and the model's role in it.
slides.visual: Follow the model-to-action-to-feedback loop in the documentation figure. Contrast it verbally with a fixed three-step script. Emphasize that a mandatory check can surround a flexible model decision.
slides.question: Does a retry loop by itself prove that the model chooses the workflow?
slides.answer: No. Code can implement a fixed retry rule. We need to see how the next action is selected.
slides.transition: That flexibility makes the task's goals and authority especially important.

slides.title: An agent needs a clear goal and limits
slides.say: A useful assignment states what the agent should achieve, which tools it may use and when it must stop. Our example permits studies and an evidence report. The operator reviews the findings and decides whether a later operating action is allowed. Review may also lead to a request for more analysis. The generic LangGraph form shows one way software can pause for outside input. It is not a utility dispatch screen. The operating process must establish the reviewer's identity, the exact case being reviewed and the permitted response. Approval of an old study should not silently become approval of a changed action or a different grid state.
slides.visual: Read the review form as a pause in a software process. Point out the information a grid-specific review would additionally need: case identity, current versions, evidence and a clearly stated proposed action.
slides.question: If a reviewer approves a report, does that automatically authorize live switching?
slides.answer: No. The scope of that approval and the separate operating permissions must be explicit.
slides.transition: We can now place retrieval, tools, memory and orchestration in the same picture.

slides.title: A model can use records, tools and memory
slides.say: Retrieval finds relevant records. Tools perform defined tasks. Memory preserves context or earlier results. An LLM can use these capabilities while working through a goal. LangGraph can coordinate the execution. PowerAgent develops power-domain models, interfaces and workflows. PowerDAG is a particular research system with its own supervisory design. These names describe different roles, so we should avoid treating them as interchangeable products. The image shows Anthropic's general augmented-model pattern. It is not a diagram of either power-system project. To judge a specific system, ask which component chooses, which component calculates, what evidence is saved and which checks the application enforces.
slides.visual: Identify retrieval, tools and memory around the central model. Give one power example for each: a manual, a power-flow service and a saved study result. Keep the architecture's attribution separate from the later research implementations.
slides.question: What is the difference between a retrieved manual and a power-flow result?
slides.answer: The manual supplies documentary evidence. The solver result supplies a calculation for specified inputs. Both need identity and scope checks.
slides.transition: Let us look at what companies actually report doing.

slides.title: PJM uses HyperQ to review connection applications
slides.say: PJM's interconnection work provides a concrete document-review example. Tapestry's June 2026 report says HyperQ entered Cycle 1 on 29 April, after PJM had confirmed testing in March. The reported Gemini agents check land-use rights, property parcels and tariff evidence for 811 generation applications. They help establish whether application materials are ready for the electrical study. Engineers retain the final decision. This is useful because a study can begin with incomplete or inconsistent evidence. It does not establish autonomous power-flow analysis. The article also discusses a future migration to Google ADK, so we should not label that future runtime as the deployed implementation.
slides.visual: Show the publisher and date in the article header. Identify the pictured animation as publisher material. Connect the document checks to the engineering inputs they precede.
slides.question: Which part of an interconnection application is being assisted here?
slides.answer: Document and readiness checks before the electrical study, with final human review.
slides.transition: The next slide asks exactly what the reported processing numbers count.

slides.title: HyperQ: what the reported numbers measure
slides.say: A numerical headline becomes useful only when we know its denominator and timing boundary. Here the supplier reports 811 applications, 4,581 raw documents and 2,328 document bundles. Checking four criteria across those bundles produces 9,312 macro-assessments. That is a count of assessments, rather than a count of projects. The displayed timings cover computer processing and exclude document transfer and human validation. We therefore cannot read the chart as the duration of the entire interconnection process. It also gives no confusion matrix from which to calculate review accuracy. When presenting an efficiency claim, name both the work completed by the system and the work that remains for people.
slides.visual: Read the unit beside each number before discussing speed. Connect 2,328 bundles times four criteria to 9,312 assessments. Point to the timing boundary stated in the caption.
slides.question: Can 9,312 assessments be described as 9,312 generation projects?
slides.answer: No. The report covers 811 applications and multiple checks per document bundle.
slides.transition: An outage-review example uses a different task and a different timing boundary.

slides.title: CAISO/OATI: agents help review planned outages
slides.say: The CAISO and OATI example concerns planned-outage review. OATI describes Workflow, Advisor and Recon agents working under a coordinator, with operators retaining authority. CAISO's July 2025 account described a pilot. OATI's later 2026 report describes daily production use and processing more than 500 next-day requests nightly in under eight minutes. That is a batch-processing claim. It implies more than 62.5 requests per minute for the reported batch, but it does not give the latency of an individual request or the remaining reviewer effort. The control-room photograph gives context. It does not independently verify the software or the performance result.
slides.visual: Identify the real control-room photo, then direct attention to the supplier-reported task and batch figures. Distinguish the pilot account from the later production-use statement.
slides.question: What measurement would help an operator judge the practical benefit?
slides.answer: End-to-end completion time and human review effort, alongside error rates and the batch processing result.
slides.transition: Planning-study preparation is another promising place to assist engineers.

slides.title: Duke and AWS: agents help prepare planning studies
slides.say: AWS reports that Duke engineers use managed agents to prepare cases and coordinate interconnection studies. The September 2026 announcement describes data preparation falling from two weeks of manual work to hours. The agents coordinate existing models, scripts and physics software. Engineers retain responsibility for the engineering decisions. The source does not specify the final number of hours, the sample count or the model and software framework. We can describe the reported change without inventing a precise speedup. Also keep the task clear: faster input preparation is one part of a longer engineering and regulatory process. The operator photograph is contextual and predates the announcement.
slides.visual: Explain that the photograph shows a Duke operator, while the reported application supports planning. On the text, emphasize data preparation as the measured boundary.
slides.question: Can we turn two weeks to hours into an exact percentage saving?
slides.answer: No. The final number of hours and the comparison conditions are unspecified.
slides.transition: Product announcements show possible integration paths, with a different level of evidence.

slides.title: Siemens announces agents for PSS E planning studies
slides.say: Siemens announces agentic planning features within Gridscale X and PSS E. The proposed agents coordinate transmission-planning simulations through software interfaces, including connection studies for data centers and other large loads. An established simulation environment offers a practical place to connect an assistant to numerical tools. The announcement does not identify a production user of those new agentic PSS E features. The same release mentions Alliander's migration to the platform, which establishes a different fact. A platform customer is not automatically a user of every newly announced capability. We should keep the feature announcement, customer adoption and measured engineering outcome separate when teaching this case.
slides.visual: Point to the original press-release header and label its evidence type as an announcement. Describe the simulation coordination concept without treating the screenshot as a live application record.
slides.question: What additional evidence would establish production use of this feature?
slides.answer: A named user and a clear account of the actual agentic feature in operation, ideally with measured outcomes.
slides.transition: A direct corporate disclosure gives us another type of use claim.

slides.title: National Grid reports agents checking project plans
slides.say: National Grid's May 2026 results transcript reports agentic checks within its capital control tower. The task is project assurance: examining early project options and documents at approval stages. Feedback arrives while project managers can still revise their plans. This is a useful example of assistance around a decision process rather than direct grid control. The transcript provides no agent framework, accuracy estimate or timing measurement. Later comments about optimizing access outages concern future work. Nearby results about other automation should not be reassigned to this agentic system. Read each claim with its own task, timing and evidence.
slides.visual: Use the slide's three statements as a sequence: project material, agent feedback, manager revision. There is no software screenshot here, so keep the explanation concrete through an example project document.
slides.question: What can we conclude from the disclosure alone?
slides.answer: The group reports using agents for project assurance. The source does not quantify their performance.
slides.transition: Good project evidence also depends on good underlying data.

slides.title: NYPA: better data for agent use
slides.say: NYPA's webinar example focuses on data quality. It describes Databricks and Ataccama checks for meter data before AI uses it. Meter records need consistent identifiers, timestamps and quality information to support later analysis. A separate demonstration links Genie to Ataccama through MCP, the Model Context Protocol. That demonstration uses a product and reorder example. We should keep the NYPA data-quality implementation distinct from the generic agent demo. Together they illustrate why agents need reliable inputs and a clear connection to data services. They do not establish a production NYPA agent issuing grid commands.
slides.visual: Identify the NYPA speaker in the original webinar artwork. Explain the separation between the meter-data discussion and the product-data demonstration.
slides.question: Why is data quality relevant even if no agent controls equipment?
slides.answer: A planning or advisory answer can still be wrong when it uses missing, duplicated or incorrectly identified data.
slides.transition: A hiring requirement can show growing interest, while supporting a narrower conclusion.

slides.title: Eversource: adding agentic skills to grid studies
slides.say: Eversource already uses MATLAB and Synergi Electric for distribution studies. A MathWorks account describes conventional Monte Carlo and parallel numerical simulations for examining many possible conditions. Separately, an October 2026 engineering vacancy asks for agentic and AI-based workflows in MATLAB. This shows the company seeking skills that could connect new workflows to existing tools. It does not show that an agentic platform has been deployed. The simulation timing improvement in the older account belongs to conventional automation. Keeping that distinction lets us discuss the motivation honestly: an established engineering environment can make agent integration plausible, while the job posting indicates capability building.
slides.visual: Show the official vacancy header and the agentic-workflow wording. Explain that the earlier simulation work and the vacancy are separate pieces of evidence.
slides.question: Does a job posting establish a deployed agentic system?
slides.answer: No. It supports hiring intent and desired engineering capabilities.
slides.transition: GE Vernova illustrates the platform context into which such capabilities might fit.

slides.title: GE Vernova: a platform that can connect grid tools
slides.say: GE Vernova's GridOS example concerns a platform for coordinating grid software and information. The public announcement names Alabama Power's use of GridOS for Distribution. Shared software can provide places to connect study tools, saved evidence and operator workflows. An agent integrated into that environment would still need clear interfaces, current case identity, engineering checks and bounded authority. The public statement does not isolate a reliability improvement caused by agents or establish an autonomous LLM controller. This case helps us think about adoption infrastructure. We should teach the difference between having an integrated platform and proving that a particular agent improves an operating task.
slides.visual: Use the control-room image to discuss where evidence could reach an operator. Describe interfaces and review as a teaching integration example rather than as verified details of the product.
slides.question: What else would we need before claiming an agent improved reliability?
slides.answer: A defined agent task and a study connecting that task to measured reliability outcomes under stated conditions.
slides.transition: Now consider the people who would review an assistant's work.

slides.title: Operators often work against a deadline
slides.say: A PNNL survey of 20 control-room operators reported that, on average, 61 percent of tasks needed completion in under 30 minutes. This is an average share of tasks, not the percentage of operators. The survey had 75 questions, but that does not create 1,500 independent timing observations. The source gives no task denominator or spread behind the 61 percent. Treat it as a small self-report study that motivates attention to deadlines. For an assistant to help, it must fit within the time available for finding, checking and acting on evidence. A fast draft that requires extensive correction may still miss that deadline.
slides.visual: Identify the real control-room context. Read the sample size, percentage and time threshold as three separate items. Ask learners to name one time-critical task they actually perform.
slides.question: Would a faster model response alone prove a better control-room tool?
slides.answer: No. We must measure the completed task, including review and correction, within its deadline.
slides.transition: We will use three checks to judge whether a recommendation is useful.

slides.title: Three checks for a useful recommendation
slides.say: The first check is data validity. Does the evidence refer to the right asset, time, units and grid connections? The second is engineering validity. Does the study solve the requested problem and meet the relevant equations and limits? The third is decision validity. Does the result justify the next action that this user is allowed to take? Each can fail independently. A well-formatted result can use yesterday's topology. A converged optimization can change a prohibited setting. A correct base-case study can leave required outages untested. These checks give us a consistent way to inspect every later paper and exercise.
slides.visual: Use the conventional situational-awareness screenshot to ask which displayed evidence would need an asset, timestamp and case identity. The three checks are tutorial teaching categories, not measured CAISO agent results.
slides.question: If a calculation converges on the wrong topology, which checks are affected?
slides.answer: The input consistency check fails, and the engineering conclusion may no longer apply to the requested grid.
slides.transition: We begin by turning a broad request into a testable assignment.

slides.title: A clear task makes success easier to test
slides.say: Suppose the user asks whether an earlier study still applies after an event. We first identify the relevant asset, event and prior result. A snapshot records the data time, topology version and model revision. The assignment should say what evidence is required and which studies are allowed. It should also specify stopping conditions: missing data, changed inputs, tool failure, exhausted budget or insufficient permission. A successful outcome might be an evidence-backed answer, or a clear request for information needed to finish. The number of tool calls or length of the report does not define success. All F12 labels and policies in this teaching example are invented.
slides.visual: Use the product screen as context for the information involved. Verbally form a request using a named case, snapshot and allowed report. Separate that invented task contract from product capabilities.
slides.question: What should the agent return if required current data cannot be obtained?
slides.answer: A clear unresolved status, the missing information and the reason the original question remains unanswered.
slides.transition: We can now follow an agent's decision loop on that assignment.

slides.title: An LLM agent acts, reads the result and decides again
slides.say: The agent acts, reads the returned evidence and decides again. Imagine that a tool confirms the asset identity but the next tool returns stale measurements. That observation should change the next step. The agent can request a refresh, ask a person or stop with an unresolved result. The surrounding software runs each tool against a specified snapshot and records what happened. A historian returns measurements. A simulator returns modeled behavior. Those outputs answer different questions, even if both arrive as structured data. Feedback in this loop means using returned evidence to choose another step. It does not necessarily mean retraining model weights or learning a new control policy.
slides.visual: Trace the published agent loop from action to tool response to the next decision. Give one normal response and one error response. Ask which path each should trigger.
slides.question: When the tool reports stale data, should the original plan continue unchanged?
slides.answer: No. The next step should address the missing current evidence or stop clearly.
slides.transition: The next example makes that stop condition explicit.

slides.title: When data are stale, the next step is to stop
slides.say: A successful asset lookup does not guarantee that all later evidence is usable. In this example, the measurement tool marks its result as stale. The system should ask for current evidence and retain the original task as unresolved. It should not replace the missing measurement with an invented value or silently reuse an older one. A trace records the requests, results and case identity so that a reviewer can inspect this behavior. The published picture illustrates a generic gate in a workflow. The gate becomes useful only when the application defines the actual test and enforces it. Saving a trace also does not make the trace correct. It makes inspection possible.
slides.visual: Follow the chain to the gate. State the invented stale-data response and ask learners to choose the next action. Keep the original source figure's generic role clear.
slides.question: What should appear in the report after the stale-data check fails?
slides.answer: The missing current evidence, affected case, reason for stopping and question that remains unresolved.
slides.transition: Even a current result can fail through a unit mismatch.

slides.title: Unit checks catch a kV versus p.u. mistake
slides.say: Per unit expresses a quantity relative to a chosen base. A measured 12.47 kilovolts equals 1.00 per unit only when the relevant voltage base is also 12.47 kilovolts and the definitions match. If an interface expects per unit, passing the number 12.47 without its unit changes its meaning. The tool should reject that request or require the information needed for an explicit conversion. Software checks should cover the unit, base and asset identity. A prompt saying use correct units is insufficient. After conversion, we still need to check whether the measurement and model are accurate. Unit checking solves one specific consistency problem.
slides.visual: Follow the wrong-value path, identify the missing base, then explain value divided by base. State the matching voltage convention before doing the simple division.
slides.question: With a matching 12.47 kV base, what is 12.47 kV in per unit?
slides.answer: 1.00 p.u. The conversion still needs the correct asset and voltage definitions.
slides.transition: The next consistency issue concerns the network itself.

slides.title: A study must match the current grid connections
slides.say: The earlier study used topology v42 with a closed switch. The event opens that switch and creates v43. The old result therefore describes a different electrical connection pattern. Updating the report's wording cannot update the voltages or flows. The application must identify the affected calculations, refresh their inputs and run them again. Matching versions is necessary but does not answer every question. We must also ask whether the model accurately represents the real grid and whether the measurements represent the event. This is why evidence should identify both its data snapshot and its model and topology revisions. A recent timestamp alone cannot establish all three.
slides.visual: Point to the changed switch in the before-and-after diagram. Trace which result belongs to v42 and which input snapshot now describes v43.
slides.question: Can an old result become valid by changing its topology label?
slides.answer: No. The affected numerical work must actually use the changed network and be checked again.
slides.transition: We also need to choose the engineering problem that answers the request.

slides.title: A solver result depends on the problem it solves
slides.say: Power flow, optimal dispatch and dynamic simulation answer different questions. Power flow calculates a steady operating condition for specified injections. Optimization chooses permitted variables to improve an objective while meeting stated constraints. A dynamic study follows the system's response over time under a model of equipment behavior. The assistant must select the study that matches the question. A solver's success status belongs to that defined problem. We still inspect numerical residuals, modeled limits, scenario coverage and permissions. A solver can converge perfectly on a problem the user never requested. The generic routing diagram helps us discuss selecting a tool, while the engineering requirements must come from the actual assignment.
slides.visual: Name one question for each study type. Then follow the routing figure and identify the information needed before selecting a branch.
slides.question: Does a successful power-flow run establish dynamic stability?
slides.answer: No. It answers a steady-state question. Dynamic stability requires an appropriate dynamic model and study.
slides.transition: Let us practice checking returned evidence before accepting a conclusion.

slides.title: Exercise 1: check three returned data packets
slides.say: Work in pairs. For this exercise, evidence must be no more than 60 seconds old, use topology v43 and express the quantity in per unit. The user may recommend actions only. Inspect packets A, B and C, choose which passes these initial rules and explain why the others fail. Then discuss the harder question: does passing these rules establish the complete engineering result or permission to execute anything? The 60-second threshold is an invented classroom rule. Your answer should use the stated contract rather than assumptions about an actual utility's procedures.
slides.visual: Keep the question visible while learners work. Advance once for the worked answer; do not show that next slide during prediction.
slides.question: Which packet passes, and what remains unproved?
slides.answer: C passes the initial age, version and unit checks. A uses v42. B uses kV. C still needs asset mapping, model and engineering validity, coverage and review. Advisory permission does not authorize execution.
slides.transition: Let us check each part of the question on the next slide.

slides.title: Exercise 1 answer: C passes the first checks
slides.say: Reveal after the pairs share their decisions. A is recent but uses v42. B is recent and uses v43, but has kV instead of p.u. C is 45 seconds old, uses v43 and has p.u. units. C passes the three stated checks only. Asset mapping, model validity, engineering checks and scenario coverage remain necessary. Recommendation permission does not authorize execution.
slides.visual: Read the diagram from each input to its result. Answer every part of the preceding exercise, then state the operator’s remaining responsibility.
slides.question: What still needs to happen before the operator can act?
slides.answer: For packet C, the remaining engineering checks and permission still apply.
slides.transition: Now connect this check to the next engineering example.

slides.title: Power-system papers test different tasks
slides.say: The papers ahead investigate several different tasks. Disturbance analysis extracts information from recorded waveforms. Simulation assistants prepare and execute numerical studies. Control prototypes propose changes in model grids. Retrieval benchmarks test whether systems can find and combine evidence correctly. Every result belongs to a particular task, tool set, allowed action space and test population. A percentage from one paper cannot rank a system against another paper that measures something else. As we proceed, use four questions: what does the agent decide, what do the tools calculate, what counts as success and which failures remain? This will make the architectures easier to compare without collapsing their different goals.
slides.visual: Treat the source photograph as research context. Ask learners to place their own task into one of the study families before introducing the first framework.
slides.question: Why should we avoid ranking all papers by their reported percentages?
slides.answer: Their tasks, datasets, scoring rules and allowed computation differ. The percentages answer different questions.
slides.transition: PowerAgent first provides a roadmap for organizing power-domain components.

slides.title: Harvard PowerAgent: models, tools and study workflows
slides.say: Harvard's PowerAgent roadmap connects three layers. PowerFM concerns models that support power-system tasks. PowerMCP concerns interfaces through which software can expose engineering tools. PowerWF concerns workflows that coordinate the work. The 2025 IEEE article is a roadmap, rather than a benchmark claiming one fixed deployment result. PowerAgentBench-Dyn is a later benchmark with its own task and evaluation rules. Keeping the initiative and the benchmark separate avoids assigning one experiment's score to the whole project. The architecture shown here comes from the authors' presentation. We inspected that presentation and the project materials, while the original article's full experimental content was unavailable. We therefore attribute no uninspected experimental result to it.
slides.visual: Walk through the three source panels in order: models, interfaces, workflows. Give a short example of each role. Cite the IEEE title and DOI in the script's source section.
slides.question: Where would an interface to an existing simulator fit in this roadmap?
slides.answer: In the tool-connection role described by PowerMCP, while the workflow controls when and how it is used.
slides.transition: A concrete PowerWF example makes these layers easier to understand.

slides.title: PowerAgent example: what changes when load is added?
slides.say: Consider a proposed load addition. The workflow analyzes an original case and a case with added load. It runs power flow and selected N minus one checks, which examine single-component outages. LangGraph coordinates the steps and saved results. PowerWorld performs the electrical calculation. That separation tells us what each component contributes: coordination, numerical analysis and evidence for comparing the cases. The maintained graph code uses StateGraph and ToolNode, but one repository does not establish the software choice for every PowerAgent project. The demonstrations provide a concrete workflow. They do not give a controlled estimate of utility time savings or operating reliability. We still need the cases, assumptions and comparison results.
slides.visual: Follow the source workflow from the load-growth request into base and changed-case studies. Point to the numerical comparison rather than treating the picture as an exact rendering of the current code.
slides.question: What changes when we add load: the language model or the electrical study inputs?
slides.answer: The electrical inputs change. The workflow must run and compare the appropriate studies for those inputs.
slides.transition: Next, a disturbance-analysis paper shows why tool order matters.

slides.title: DrAgent: reading a recorded grid fault
slides.say: DrAgent studies recorded disturbances on transmission lines. First look at the waveform before discussing any AI component. The third current trace changes sharply during the fault. The marked locations identify inception, the highest current and clearance, when the fault ends. A tool can return a sample index or a current measurement. An engineering answer still needs to translate that output into the requested quantity and units. Locating a visible spike is a different question from interpreting its physical cause or assessing equipment. The figure is an original research record, rather than an invented control-room event. We will next connect the waveform questions to the tools that answer them.
slides.visual: Locate the third trace. Point to the start, peak and clearance markers in that order. Explain that the horizontal position represents time or sample location and the vertical value represents current.
slides.question: Would the highest current sample alone tell us the fault duration?
slides.answer: No. Duration needs a start and an end, with the appropriate timing information.
slides.transition: The architecture assigns those subtasks to particular tools.

slides.title: DrAgent selects tools to answer a fault question
slides.say: DrAgent uses a ReWOO-based plan to choose domain functions and document search. ReWOO plans tool work using references to results that earlier steps will produce. In this implementation, Gemini 1.5 Pro plans, about a dozen domain functions analyze signals, and retrieval searches 138 product manuals. Recorded disturbance files use the COMTRADE format. Notice the two different evidence paths. Signal functions measure the event, while manual search supplies product information. A question about a fault's start time may need its sample index and the recording's sampling rate before conversion to seconds. That requirement is a dependency between calculations, which gives us a reason to introduce task graphs.
slides.visual: Follow the planning stage into signal analysis and manual search, then back into the response. Explain RAG as finding relevant source passages for the model.
slides.question: Which two inputs are needed to turn a sample index into a time offset?
slides.answer: The index under the tool's indexing convention and the sampling rate. A record start time is also needed for an absolute timestamp.
slides.transition: Before graph design, inspect what this tool-based approach achieved.

slides.title: DrAgent: more correct answers, with errors still present
slides.say: The chart reconstructs correct-answer counts from the paper's individual score cells. Across 18 recorded cases, fault-inception answers increase from 12 to 18, and maximum-current answers from 16 to 18. The timing category increases from four to 13. Here we count scores of two or above as correct under the authors' rubric. The timing category also accepts a correctly labeled duration, so it is broader than exact clearance timestamps. A domain expert graded the answers using the paper's tolerances of three milliseconds for timing and five percent for current. These are author-data-derived counts, rather than a new experiment. They show useful gains on this task while leaving errors and a small test population.
slides.visual: Read the denominator before the bars. Compare the timing bars last, then identify the remaining five cases. Mention the audited counts rather than the inconsistent printed Q6 mean.
slides.question: Does 18 out of 18 establish general fault-analysis reliability?
slides.answer: No. It describes the tested records and grading rule. Other records and tasks remain to be evaluated.
slides.transition: The tool sequence becomes clearer once we distinguish three kinds of graph.

slides.title: Three kinds of graph have different jobs
slides.say: The first graph is the electrical network. Its edges represent physical connections between modeled components. The second is a task dependency graph. Its edges say which calculation needs an earlier result. The third is an execution workflow. Its edges determine which software step can run next, and it may contain retry loops. These are different objects. A radial feeder can have a tree-like electrical shape while its software repeatedly revisits a diagnostic step. A calculation DAG can analyze a meshed electrical network. When someone says a node or a loop, ask which graph they mean. This prevents a software architecture picture from being mistaken for the grid model.
slides.visual: Compare the three panels. Name one node and the meaning of one edge in each. Point out the loop in the workflow and its absence from the task DAG.
slides.question: Does a loop in the software imply that the electrical feeder is meshed?
slides.answer: No. Software execution and electrical connectivity are separate structures.
slides.transition: Now use the fault example to read an actual dependency graph.

slides.title: A DAG shows which result must come first
slides.say: A directed acyclic graph, or DAG, connects tasks without forming a directed loop. An arrow means the downstream calculation needs the upstream result. To convert a fault-start sample into a time, we first need the sample index and the sampling rate. A peak-current calculation may run independently when it uses the same unchanged record and does not need the timing result. A valid execution order respects every required dependency. The page position of a box does not determine its order. Before reporting, the application must wait for all required outputs or clearly identify what is missing. This is a practical way to reason about both correctness and possible parallel work.
slides.visual: Trace both arrows into the time conversion. Then follow the separate peak-current branch. Ask learners to identify a valid order without relying on left-to-right box placement.
slides.question: Can the time conversion run as soon as the sample index arrives?
slides.answer: Only if the required sampling-rate information is already available and matches the same record.
slides.transition: LangGraph manages execution, which can include more than an acyclic task plan.

slides.title: LangGraph can pause to inspect a run
slides.say: LangGraph is software for defining state and running workflow nodes with edges and routing rules. A node can call fixed code, a simulator or an LLM. Unlike a DAG, the execution can revisit a step. A debugger can pause the graph so a developer can inspect progress. That static breakpoint differs from a dynamic interrupt that requests external input. StateGraph defines stored fields, while application reducers determine how parallel updates combine. Those facilities help implement a process. The application still defines data validation, engineering tests, permissions and stopping conditions. Executing the graph successfully cannot establish that the electrical model or the chosen study is valid.
slides.visual: Explain the highlighted debug pause as a developer inspection point. Use a short run-check-repair example to describe a loop, then distinguish it from human review.
slides.question: Does using LangGraph automatically add a power-system feasibility check?
slides.answer: No. The application must call and interpret the appropriate engineering tools and enforce the requirements.
slides.transition: Those tools produce evidence that the workflow must keep identifiable.

slides.title: Saved state must identify the study and its evidence
slides.say: Saved state should identify the study, its input versions, results, status and attempt count. Suppose a set of parallel outage studies expects a case called outage_34. The application needs to notice if that result is missing or appears twice. A generic state store does not automatically understand that engineering requirement. Reducers or an external evidence store must preserve the case identities and combine updates correctly. A list of three completed steps is insufficient if the requested set contained four cases. Save enough information to compare the expected set with the returned evidence. That makes both missing coverage and inappropriate reuse easier to detect.
slides.visual: Read the figure as generic software state. Describe expected-case and returned-case sets verbally. Make clear that those grid-specific fields are tutorial design requirements.
slides.question: What should the report do when one required outage result is absent?
slides.answer: Name the missing case and retain an incomplete or unresolved status for conclusions that depend on it.
slides.transition: Saved progress also allows a run to pause and resume.

slides.title: A checkpoint lets a workflow pause and resume
slides.say: A checkpoint records workflow progress. A thread identifier links saved steps to the same run so execution can resume later. However, external conditions may change during a pause. A saved voltage result may no longer match the current topology. The application must revalidate the snapshot and rerun affected work. There is another software detail to consider: the interrupted node may restart from its beginning. Actions before the pause may therefore run again. Stable step IDs or idempotency controls can prevent a repeated request from applying the same change twice. Saving and resuming software state solves a coordination problem. It does not keep the external grid state frozen.
slides.visual: Follow the checkpoint sequence across the pause. Ask what could change outside the software before resumption. Explain idempotency as safely recognizing a repeated operation.
slides.question: Can resuming a saved thread justify reusing every old numerical result?
slides.answer: No. Reuse depends on whether each result's relevant inputs still match.
slides.transition: The same identity checks matter when several studies run together.

slides.title: Parallel outage studies must account for every case
slides.say: Parallel studies can reduce waiting when the cases are independent. Each selected outage should run on a consistent copy of the same starting case. Afterward, the application must compare the expected case IDs with the returned results. A failed or missing branch remains unresolved. An aggregator that summarizes only successful branches can produce an attractive but incomplete report. If a case called C2 fails, the report should identify C2, its error and the conclusions that cannot yet be drawn. Even completing every selected case does not imply that the selected set covers every relevant single-component outage. Coverage has to match the original assignment.
slides.visual: Trace the generic fan-out and fan-in figure. Verbally remove one branch result and ask what the aggregator must preserve rather than summarize away.
slides.question: If two out of three required studies finish, can the report declare all selected outages acceptable?
slides.answer: No. It can report those two results while explicitly leaving the third case and affected conclusions unresolved.
slides.transition: PowerDAG addresses a related problem: calling a tool before its prerequisites exist.

slides.title: PowerDAG checks the steps needed before a tool runs
slides.say: PowerDAG retrieves relevant verified workflow examples and uses a dependency graph with a supervisory gate. The gate checks required earlier tool calls before allowing another tool to run. The inspected version four covers 108 tools, ten task families and four Vermont feeder models. Those are distribution networks: Rochester, Stowe, Glover and South Hero. The agent still chooses steps, while the supervisor constrains their order. This combines flexible selection with explicit workflow rules. The exact gate matters. In this paper it checks encoded prior Write-tool names. That is narrower than checking every parameter, input version or physical consequence. We should explain the gate's actual guarantee before interpreting its benchmark result.
slides.visual: Follow the agent's proposed call through the supervisor and into the environment. Show where retrieval supplies examples and where the prerequisite check occurs.
slides.question: Can a prerequisite-name gate alone prove that a result uses the current topology?
slides.answer: No. Freshness and parameter consistency need additional checks that identify the actual inputs and outputs.
slides.transition: The voltage example makes that boundary concrete.

slides.title: PowerDAG: solve the grid before checking its voltage
slides.say: A voltage-violation check needs a solved network state. If the required earlier solver step is missing, the gate rejects the call and explains what needs to happen first. That prevents one important class of workflow error. Now ask a second question: did that solve use the current network? The paper's check of executed tool names does not by itself establish freshness. Our teaching diagram adds a current-v43 condition to show the stronger requirement an application may need. It is labeled as an adaptation. Passing a dependency gate therefore means the encoded prerequisites passed. The numerical solution and the resulting engineering conclusion still require their own checks.
slides.visual: Read the missing-prerequisite path first, then the permitted path. Point explicitly to the added v43 freshness condition so learners do not attribute it to the paper's original gate.
slides.question: If solve appears in the history, what else would you want before checking voltage?
slides.answer: Evidence that the solve used the required case and current inputs, returned an appropriate status and produced the needed results.
slides.transition: Now interpret the controlled benchmark without enlarging that guarantee.

slides.title: PowerDAG results: the same queries, four setups
slides.say: This comparison uses the same GPT-5.5 model and 150 test queries in each setup. The reported first-run workflow success is 77.33 percent for ReAct, 92.67 for retrieval only, 96 for just-in-time supervision only and 98 for full PowerDAG. Pass at one checks required tool coverage, compatible inputs and ordering against expert workflows. Each query runs once in each setup. These held-out queries still come from the same ten task families. The comparison supports the value of these complete configurations on that benchmark. It does not measure reliability of live commands or isolate the effect of one graph edge. Keep the model, task population and score definition attached to the headline.
slides.visual: Read the same-model label and denominator before comparing bars. Explain retrieval only and supervision only as separate tested setups. Finish by defining what the 98 percent actually measures.
slides.question: Does 98 percent workflow Pass@1 mean a 98 percent chance of safe field operation?
slides.answer: No. It measures the specified first-run workflow criteria on the benchmark queries.
slides.transition: Reproducibility also depends on what the public release contains.

slides.title: PowerDAG: what can others check and reuse?
slides.say: The PowerDAG public benchmark provides tasks, tool descriptions, workflow records and scoring code. That allows others to inspect the study design and some of the execution evidence. The release has a practical boundary: BESS, basicPV and GFI can run from the public files, while seven other task families need private feeder maps, geographic data and network-tool code. Public records are therefore useful without making the entire study independently runnable from the download. When reusing the idea, we can adopt explicit prerequisite checks and then test them against our own tools and state rules. We should not assume that a published gate automatically transfers unchanged to a different utility environment.
slides.visual: Count the three public task families and the seven with external dependencies verbally. Point learners to the linked paper and repository rather than promising a one-click full reproduction.
slides.question: What can we reuse even when every dataset is unavailable?
slides.answer: The design idea, task and tool descriptions, available workflow evidence and scoring approach, followed by new validation for the intended environment.
slides.transition: Another paper focuses on generating and repairing simulation code.

slides.title: Simulation agents find functions, run code and repair errors
slides.say: The feedback-driven simulation framework finds relevant MATLAB functions and settings, writes code and runs it. Tool errors return feedback that can guide repair. The study uses DALINE and MATPOWER tasks. This illustrates a real agentic role: selecting and correcting the steps needed to complete a simulation request. However, a program can run without matching the requested engineering settings. We must compare the executed study with the assignment, including required variables and unnecessary changes. A successful software exit is one layer of evidence. Numerical and task-level checks are additional layers. The paper does not identify LangGraph, so we should describe its workflow without assigning an unreported software framework.
slides.visual: Follow the source feedback path from generated code to execution and back to repair. Give an example of code running with the wrong setting and ask where that error would be detected.
slides.question: Is no MATLAB error a sufficient success criterion?
slides.answer: No. The study and settings must also satisfy the requested engineering task.
slides.transition: The scoring rule in this paper makes that distinction particularly important.

slides.title: Simulation-agent results: points, not a pass rate
slides.say: For 34 DALINE tasks, each graded attempt receives 100 points if it meets every requirement without extra settings, 50 if unnecessary settings remain and zero if a requirement is missed. The score averages allowed attempt slots, carrying the final score into unused slots. The full setup reports 93.13 on this scale. It is not a statement that 93.13 percent of tasks passed. Other shown setups score zero, 31.37 and 33.82. These compare complete systems with different retrieval and feedback arrangements, including a separate ChatGPT product setup. The related MATPOWER test reports 96.85 over 35 tasks with up to five attempts. Always explain the score before comparing its height.
slides.visual: Read the horizontal-axis metric and the 100/50/0 rubric aloud. Compare the full setup with the others only after explaining the attempt averaging.
slides.question: Can we multiply 34 tasks by 93.13 percent to recover a number of successful tasks?
slides.answer: No. The graded attempt-averaged score is not a completion fraction.
slides.transition: Repeated feedback can help, but it can also preserve a software mistake.

slides.title: Trying again can repeat the same software error
slides.say: A capability study found an error involving a 100 megawatt and 10 megavar load request. The agent request omitted reactive load, and the cache key omitted it as well. Correcting the request still returned the old result because the cache could not distinguish the corrected input. A cache stores earlier results for reuse. Its key must include the inputs that determine whether reuse is valid. In this case, trying again with better wording cannot repair the underlying key. The lesson extends to model revisions, topology and other relevant settings. Agent evaluation needs to test adapters and caching behavior as well as model responses. A fluent explanation can repeatedly describe the same stale calculation.
slides.visual: Use the evaluator loop as a generic feedback picture. Narrate the original request, corrected request and unchanged cache result. Ask which software component must change.
slides.question: Why did correcting the prompt fail to obtain a fresh result?
slides.answer: The cache key ignored a result-changing input. The adapter and cache needed correction, not another verbal retry.
slides.transition: Let us make these loops visible in two official platform demonstrations.

slides.title: LangGraph Studio: watch an agent use tools
slides.say: This official walkthrough makes an agent run visible. Watch the graph, the selected tool and the returned result. The platform can pause a run and inspect its saved state. In a power-system application, the numerical solver would be one of these tools. The model coordinates the request; the solver computes the electrical result; the operator decides what to do. This is the original 2024 Studio interface, not evidence of a utility deployment.
slides.visual: Click Play official demo. Follow one visible request through the agent graph. Pause when a tool result or delegation event is shown. Use the direct watch link if presenting in a separate tab. Ask learners to name the tool, result and next decision; do not treat the demo as grid validation.
slides.question: Where would you pause this workflow to check a power-flow result?
slides.answer: After the solver returns and before a recommendation is accepted. Check convergence, units and the study inputs.
slides.transition: Now compare how work and evidence move through the next example.

slides.title: Siemens PSS E: agentic transmission planning
slides.say: Play the full 79-second product video linked from Siemens’ agentic transmission-planning page. This is a supplier overview of Gridscale X PSS E, rather than a complete recorded engineering study. Connect its planning message to three separate jobs: preparing a study, computing the electrical result and interpreting it. The solver remains essential. In our lab we inspect those steps explicitly. A product video alone does not establish field accuracy or deployment at a named utility.
slides.visual: Play the full 79-second Siemens product video. Then connect its planning message to study preparation, the PSS E solver and engineering review. Ask learners which inputs and numerical checks are needed. The overview does not display a complete tool-call trace.
slides.question: Which part must still be checked by a power engineer?
slides.answer: The study inputs, the solver’s convergence and limits, and whether the result supports the proposed decision.
slides.transition: Return to power-system studies: keep the same question about who supplies and checks each result.

slides.title: GridMind 2025 connects typed agents to solvers
slides.say: The 2025 GridMind study uses PydanticAI to structure agents and pandapower for AC OPF and outage studies. It tests 14-, 30-, 118- and 300-bus systems. On case 118, the paper reports 100 percent ACOPF success across six models, with timing distributions based on five repeats. Structured types help make inputs and outputs machine-readable, but they do not establish that every required outage was studied or interpreted correctly. Keep that task boundary attached to the result. Also keep this 2025 system separate from the 2026 weather-risk GridMind workflow that we discuss next. They share a name while using different architectures and addressing different tasks.
slides.visual: Trace the typed-agent architecture into the solver. State the year and the ACOPF task explicitly. Do not infer an undisclosed success denominator from the timing sample.
slides.question: Does valid structured output prove complete contingency analysis?
slides.answer: No. We need the requested case list, returned evidence and an independent coverage check.
slides.transition: The paper's reported answers show why agreement alone is insufficient.

slides.title: GridMind: reported answers need independent checks
slides.say: For case 118, one model reports 165 percent maximum overload and five report 137 percent. The models also identify different critical lines. These are different model setups, not six repeats that estimate one model's error probability. The table provides no complete independent outage reference that would tell us which answer covers the full required scope. A majority answer may be shared, incomplete or based on different selections. The response screenshot itself is an example of agent output, rather than ground truth. To resolve the discrepancy, obtain the same case definitions and run or inspect an independent reference study. Count agreement only after establishing what the answers were supposed to cover.
slides.visual: Use the response screenshot to distinguish a reported claim from its supporting evidence. Compare the overload figures verbally and ask what reference is missing.
slides.question: Can five agreeing models establish that 137 percent is correct?
slides.answer: No. Agreement does not replace independent evidence for the same defined study scope.
slides.transition: The later GridMind study concentrates on state reuse across a weather workflow.

slides.title: GridMind 2026 reuses results when their inputs still match
slides.say: The 2026 GridMind workflow coordinates five stages using LangGraph: weather, outages, ACOPF, screening and cascade analysis. Weather comes from AERIS. Base OPF uses LUMINA or pandapower. A LUMINA surrogate provides faster screening, and EPFast uses a reduced-order DC model for cascade simulation. Input fingerprints identify when a saved result can be reused. A fingerprint is a hash of declared inputs. It can show whether those inputs match an earlier run, but it cannot detect an important input that was never included. Dependencies must reflect the actual implementation. Here the contingency stage reads outage schedules directly, so a change in the ACOPF solver does not automatically invalidate every stage that appears later in a list.
slides.visual: Walk through the five named stages verbally. For each, name its output and which later work actually consumes that output. Distinguish a surrogate from a detailed physics calculation.
slides.question: What must a fingerprint include to support safe reuse of a numerical result?
slides.answer: Every declared input that can change that result, including the relevant model, settings and external data versions.
slides.transition: Let us use specific input changes to read those dependencies.

slides.title: GridMind: which changes need a new run?
slides.say: If only the cascade parameter k changes, this implementation reruns cascade and reuses the unaffected results. If the forecast initialization shifts by six hours, all five stages rerun. A change of ACOPF solver reruns ACOPF only in this particular implementation because its other stages do not all consume that output. These examples show why a workflow's dependency structure matters more than a simple left-to-right sequence. Returning to exactly matching inputs can permit reuse of an earlier result. That reuse still depends on the key recording every relevant input. Another workflow may have different dependencies, so these rules should travel with the implementation rather than become universal weather-study rules.
slides.visual: Trace the highlighted invalidation paths for each change. Explain why an arrow represents actual data dependence, rather than visual proximity.
slides.question: If only k changes, should all five stages rerun under the cited design?
slides.answer: No. Cascade reruns, while results whose relevant inputs still match may be retained.
slides.transition: Reusing fewer stages can save time, but the two percentages need separate measurements.

slides.title: GridMind results: fewer stages and less time are different
slides.say: For the same seven-query session, the paper reports a 60 percent reduction in stage runs and about a 52.7 percent reduction in total run time. Those quantities differ because stages have different costs. Avoid calling a 60 percent reduction in stage count a 60 percent time saving. The gain comes from workflow design and appropriate reuse, rather than simply from a faster language model. The study reports one seven-query session and gives no repeated-session interval for the time reduction. It also uses surrogate and reduced-order models. We can learn a useful design principle while retaining those evaluation limits and the need for engineering validation.
slides.visual: Read stage executions and elapsed time as separate panels or quantities. Ask which stages dominate time and what additional measurements would establish variability.
slides.question: Why need the time saving differ from the reduction in stage count?
slides.answer: The omitted and retained stages can take different amounts of time, and execution overhead also contributes.
slides.transition: We will practice choosing which saved results still apply.

slides.title: Exercise 2: check whether saved weather-risk results still apply
slides.say: Start from a saved run with forecast F0, topology v43 and cascade parameter k equal to 50. First, change only k to 200 and decide which stages need new results. Next, shift the forecast initialization by six hours. Use the dependencies we just discussed, rather than assuming every implementation behaves the same way. Finally, imagine a required simulation fails. Decide what the operator should receive and which conclusion remains unsupported. Work from the specific cited workflow. F0 and v43 are invented classroom labels. The goal is to identify the valid evidence set and communicate any gap clearly.
slides.visual: Keep the question visible while learners work. Advance once for the worked answer; do not show that next slide during prediction.
slides.question: What reruns, and how should a failed required stage be reported?
slides.answer: Only k changed: rerun cascade. Forecast shifted: rerun all five. A failure requires incomplete or unresolved status with case and stage IDs, input versions, error and missing conclusions.
slides.transition: Let us check each part of the question on the next slide.

slides.title: Exercise 2 answer: rerun what changed
slides.say: Reveal after group discussion. Only k changing leaves the four other stage inputs unchanged in the cited trace. Shifting forecast initialization affects all five stages. A failed required simulation cannot support an all-clear report. Preserve the input versions, failed stage, tool error and any conclusions that remain unsupported.
slides.visual: Read the diagram from each input to its result. Answer every part of the preceding exercise, then state the operator’s remaining responsibility.
slides.question: What still needs to happen before the operator can act?
slides.answer: Required studies must complete and their evidence must match the case. Report unresolved work explicitly.
slides.transition: Now connect this check to the next engineering example.

slides.title: PowerAgentBench-Dyn allows only specific model changes
slides.say: PowerAgentBench-Dyn is a Harvard-led benchmark, separate from the broader PowerAgent roadmap. In its model-quality task, an agent receives a modified solar-PV dynamic model that fails eight quality tests. DMView and PSS/E provide feedback. The agent may change only four REECAU1 controller gains, with all other fields locked and at most five parameter updates. A gain changes a controller's response within the simulation model. The benchmark asks whether a tool-using agent can repair that specified model under clear constraints. It does not authorize changing a utility's live controller. The public harness also needs licensed PSS/E and external DMView software, which matters for audience expectations about reproduction.
slides.visual: Follow the source benchmark cycle from permitted parameter edits to tests and feedback. Identify the locked fields and update budget as part of the task definition.
slides.question: Why is the allowed four-gain set part of the success criterion?
slides.answer: A solution obtained by changing prohibited fields would solve a different task, even if the test outputs improved.
slides.transition: The results distinguish completing the test suite from the amount of search needed.

slides.title: PowerAgentBench-Dyn results: passed sessions and updates
slides.say: Each session passes only when all eight quality tests pass within five allowed updates. On the one modified solar-PV model, the paper reports 10 successful sessions out of 10 for Opus 4.8, 10 out of 10 for Sonnet 4.6 and nine out of 10 for Haiku 4.5. Median updates are one, one and two. The left-hand counts describe complete compliant sessions, while the right-hand values describe update effort. They are different measures. Testing one modified model limits generalization, and the study gives no matched human or fixed-search baseline. These results therefore do not establish a comparative speedup or fleet-wide model-repair reliability.
slides.visual: Read the success counts first, including the single failed session. Then read the median-update panel and explain that it does not include all operator work.
slides.question: Does a median of one update tell us the total human time saved?
slides.answer: No. It describes model-update effort in this test, not an end-to-end comparison with human work.
slides.transition: The same benchmark also includes a distinct dynamic-security task.

slides.title: PowerAgentBench-Dyn also checks grid response to faults
slides.say: The dynamic-security task uses PowerMCP and PowerFactory to study ten candidate faults and identify three critical cases. Full-workflow success also requires correct findings and staying within the allowed synchronous-condenser mitigation options. Across six models, reported passes range from zero out of ten to ten out of ten. Opus 4.7 and Sonnet 4.6 each pass nine, Haiku 4.5 passes seven, Gemini 3.1 Pro and GPT-5.5 each pass ten, and Qwen 2.5-Coder-7B passes zero. This task uses Opus 4.7, which differs from the model-quality task's Opus 4.8. A run can fail at tool execution before reaching an engineering finding. Keep those failure stages separate.
slides.visual: Explain the study as fault execution, identification and constrained mitigation. Read complete-workflow counts without combining them with the previous model-repair sessions.
slides.question: Can these counts be combined with the previous slide into one general reliability rate?
slides.answer: No. The tasks, model versions and pass criteria differ.
slides.transition: Now compare a different tool-based power-system assistant, VeraGrid-Agent.

slides.title: VeraGrid-Agent uses solver results to answer a question
slides.say: VeraGrid-Agent writes feeder inputs, runs AC optimal power flow in VeraGrid and reads the relevant output rows. Within a fixed budget it can repair tool errors, then return a multiple-choice answer. The benchmark uses 33 templates and 150 questions on one balanced radial eight-bus feeder, with 50 questions at each of three difficulty levels. Reference answers come from the same solver and circuit. The task tests whether the complete tool-using setup answers those questions accurately. It does not establish a general feeder-control policy. The same numerical study can succeed while the agent reads the wrong row, so solving and interpreting remain separate failure points.
slides.visual: Trace input writing, solving, reading and final answering in the source workflow. Identify the one-feeder and multiple-choice boundaries.
slides.question: If the solver succeeds, can the final answer still be wrong?
slides.answer: Yes. The agent may read or interpret the wrong result, use the wrong quantity or return the wrong answer choice.
slides.transition: The comparison shows the value of that whole tool-assisted setup on its defined questions.

slides.title: VeraGrid-Agent results: the same models with and without tools
slides.say: The chart compares the same named models with and without the solver-agent arrangement on 150 questions. GPT-5.2 rises from 64 correct answers to 149. Claude Sonnet 4.5 rises from 71 to 149, and Gemini 3 Flash from 74 to 150. The no-tool setup receives feeder and distributed-resource information, while the agent adds solver execution, reading tools and repeated feedback. This is a comparison of complete systems with different computation, rather than an isolated estimate of one feature's effect. The questions all use one feeder, and repeated-run variation is unspecified. The remaining errors and task boundary matter even when a bar is close to the maximum.
slides.visual: Read every pair with its denominator, then point to the one-feeder caption. Ask what additional tests would be needed for another feeder or operating task.
slides.question: Does 150 out of 150 establish general feeder dispatch performance?
slides.answer: No. It establishes the reported answer count on this fixed benchmark, with its solver, circuit and question templates.
slides.transition: The next study shows why staying within the assigned decision space matters.

slides.title: AgentiGrid: what does one reported run mean?
slides.say: AgentiGrid connects an agent to ExaGO for numerical grid-planning studies. The paper tests four models on three applications: dispatch exploration, outage screening and studies with uncertain inputs. Those combinations produce 12 different searches on one 200-bus model. They are not 12 repeats of the same task. A run without a fatal JSON error has shown that an interface exchange worked, but the complete task can still fail. We must check allowed changes, coverage of the requested cases and faithful interpretation of solver evidence. This paper is useful because its reported examples expose those different failure modes within an otherwise functioning software process.
slides.visual: Follow the prototype architecture into ExaGO. State four models times three applications as the source of the 12 setups, then separate interface execution from engineering completion.
slides.question: Can 12 different searches estimate the repeatability of one fixed task and setup?
slides.answer: No. They describe different configurations and applications.
slides.transition: One search found a lower objective by changing the problem itself.

slides.title: A lower cost can come from solving the wrong task
slides.say: The reported objective falls from 27,564 to 17,398, a reduction of about 36.9 percent in unspecified objective units. That looks attractive until we inspect the allowed changes. The task permitted dispatch changes, meaning the outputs of units already selected to operate. The model changed unit commitment, meaning which units are on. The equation shows why a larger decision set can have an equal or lower minimum. It gives the optimizer more choices. That lower value therefore does not prove improvement on the original dispatch-only task. First verify the permitted action space, then compare the objective under the same constraints and study conditions.
slides.visual: Read the subset relation as one allowed decision set being contained in a larger set. Explain the minimum inequality in words, then connect it to dispatch versus commitment.
slides.question: Why can a numerically lower objective still fail the task?
slides.answer: It may use prohibited decisions or a different constraint set, so it no longer answers the assigned optimization problem.
slides.transition: Incomplete outage coverage creates another task-level failure.

slides.title: Successful tool calls can still miss a critical outage
slides.say: All four reported outage searches find the highest-cost outage, involving lines 187 to 189. Three find the infeasible outage 29 to 30. None finds the second infeasible outage, 15 to 16. Here infeasible means that the specified study has no solution meeting its constraints. Finding the expensive outage does not establish that the search found every critical case. These are four different model setups on one grid, so we should not calculate a stable failure probability from them. The concrete lesson is to compare the required case set with the investigated set and independently check the findings. A record of successful tool calls can still hide missing engineering coverage.
slides.visual: Read across the coverage chart by required finding. Point to the missed infeasible outage and ask whether a success-only summary would expose it.
slides.question: What evidence would reveal that a critical case was never studied?
slides.answer: The expected-case list, actual returned case IDs and an independent reference or coverage check.
slides.transition: We also need counts and uncertainty when repeated attempts are available.

slides.title: Show both trial counts and uncertainty
slides.say: The capability study reports ten attempts for each shown setup on synthetic 100- and 1,000-bus grids. Six cells have ten successes out of ten and two have five out of ten. Our plotted Wilson intervals illustrate uncertainty under an independent pass/fail model at fixed settings. The paper reports the counts, rather than these calculated intervals. That statistical assumption is not established for every agent workflow. Some higher-complexity tasks and larger grids have no reported result cells in the tested version. Missing evidence should stay missing, rather than become a zero-valued result. Later software fixes also need a new set of measurements before they can support a new numerical performance claim.
slides.visual: Read the counts and whiskers separately. Identify blank or unreported conditions explicitly. Explain that the intervals are tutorial calculations rather than author-provided measurements.
slides.question: Is an unreported result equivalent to zero successes?
slides.answer: No. It is missing evidence. Zero successes would require an actual stated set of failed trials.
slides.transition: Not all benchmarks solve equations. Some test whether agents can assemble the right evidence.

slides.title: PowerBench finds answers across linked records
slides.say: PowerBench tests retrieval and reasoning over synthetic asset records, documents and time-series data. It has 300 questions in three groups of 60, 90 and 150. The generated collection covers 761 devices and 24,939 documents. Tools search, read and run Python under budgets of 50 tool calls and 300 seconds per attempt. An answer may look well formed yet refer to the wrong asset or time period, making this relevant to evidence work. However, the test does not run power flow or validate operating actions. At the recorded review, the linked repository did not provide a verified runnable release. Explain the benchmark's design without promising an immediately reproducible lab.
slides.visual: Follow the source figure from the linked records into question answering. Point out the identity and time relationships that a correct answer must preserve.
slides.question: What kind of operator task is closest to this benchmark?
slides.answer: Finding and combining evidence about assets, events or time periods, rather than calculating physical grid behavior.
slides.transition: Its different scoring rules answer different questions about those answers.

slides.title: PowerBench results: complete answers and partial credit
