slides.say: Joint accuracy requires the complete answer to have every required field and the correct format. Field accuracy gives partial credit when some fields are correct. Macro joint accuracy gives each of the three task groups equal weight. These measures can differ even for the same model responses. The chart's intervals are the authors' bootstrap intervals, obtained by resampling their data. They describe the reported metric and sampling method. Overlap between two separate model intervals does not by itself decide whether a paired model difference is statistically significant. For teaching, focus first on whether the metric matches the operator's need for a complete evidence packet or for partially useful fields.
slides.visual: Identify the joint-accuracy and field-accuracy marks using the legend. Read the axis as a reported score and the whiskers as uncertainty for that score.
slides.question: Can high field accuracy coexist with incomplete answers?
slides.answer: Yes. Many individual fields may be correct while too few answers satisfy every required field together.
slides.transition: The group breakdown makes another weakness visible.

slides.title: A strong average can hide a weak task group
slides.say: The leading row reports joint accuracies of 85.0, 88.9 and 48.7 percent in the three task groups. Their equal-weight average is about 74.2 percent. The largest group, Comparative Retrieval and Reasoning, has fewer than half of its answers completely correct. Equal weighting gives the 60-question group the same influence as the 150-question group. That is a deliberate metric choice, but it answers a different question from pooling all 300 questions. In a pilot, identify which task group matters to the operator and show that group directly. A strong average cannot stand in for acceptable performance on every required task.
slides.visual: Use the source task-family figure to name the three kinds of question. Say each group accuracy before the average, then emphasize the comparative group's lower value.
slides.question: Would an average of 74.2 percent establish acceptable performance on the comparative task?
slides.answer: No. That group's reported joint accuracy is 48.7 percent and needs to be judged separately.
slides.transition: Small trial counts create a further limit even when the observed fraction is perfect.

slides.title: What do ten successful trials tell us?
slides.say: Ten successes out of ten gives an observed success fraction of 100 percent. Under a fixed-setting independent-trial model, the calculated two-sided Wilson 95 percent interval is about 72.2 to 100 percent. Five successes out of ten gives about 23.7 to 76.3 percent. These wide intervals show how little precision a small sample provides. In repeated comparable experiments, the method aims to cover the fixed success probability 95 percent of the time. It does not assign a 95 percent probability to a fixed parameter after this one interval has been observed. Different tasks, shared errors and changed settings create additional uncertainty beyond that model.
slides.visual: Read the two count-and-interval examples slowly. Emphasize the denominator of ten and distinguish a reported fraction from its uncertainty under assumptions.
slides.question: Does a 10 out of 10 result show the true success probability is exactly one?
slides.answer: No. It is a small observed sample, and the calculation still depends on the trial model and tested population.
slides.transition: A multi-step task also depends on how its steps succeed together.

slides.title: More required steps can lower overall reliability
slides.say: Suppose each of 20 required steps succeeds independently with probability 0.99. The chance that all succeed is 0.99 raised to 20, about 81.8 percent. The curve illustrates why strong individual steps can still produce a weaker complete workflow. Real errors may share a cause, such as the wrong input snapshot, cache or adapter. In that case the simple independent-step formula does not describe the system. The exact probability chain uses conditional probabilities. Retrying a step may also repeat the same error rather than provide a fresh independent chance. Measure complete tasks and inspect failure stages instead of predicting a utility's reliability from assumed per-step rates.
slides.visual: Follow the 99-percent curve to 20 steps. Explain that all required steps must succeed for this example. State the independence assumption before using the result.
slides.question: Why might a second attempt fail for the same reason as the first?
slides.answer: It may reuse the same wrong context, stale result or defective tool adapter.
slides.transition: What we count in the final evaluation matters just as much.

slides.title: The answer changes when we change what we count
slides.say: This invented example has 80 feasible and 20 infeasible cases. The system accepts 70 feasible cases and rejects ten. It also wrongly accepts two infeasible cases and correctly rejects 18. Among all 100 cases, two false approvals are two percent. Among the 20 infeasible cases, the false-approval rate is ten percent. Among the 72 accepted cases, 70 are feasible, or 97.2 percent. Overall classification accuracy is 88 percent. Each number is arithmetically valid, but each answers a different question. For an operator, false approval of an infeasible case may matter differently from unnecessary rejection of a feasible one. Define those errors before selecting the headline metric.
slides.visual: Walk through all four outcome counts in the graphic. For each percentage, name the denominator aloud. Ask learners which error they would investigate first for their chosen task.
slides.question: What is the denominator for the false-approval rate among infeasible cases?
slides.answer: Twenty. Two wrongly accepted infeasible cases out of 20 gives ten percent.
slides.transition: Even seeing no failures needs a careful interpretation.

slides.title: Zero test failures do not prove perfect performance
slides.say: If a fixed system fails independently with probability p on each comparable trial, the chance of seeing zero failures in n trials is one minus p, raised to n. Set that chance to 0.05 and solve for p. The result is the exact one-sided 95 percent upper confidence bound: one minus 0.05 raised to one over n. With 300 zero-failure trials, the bound is about 0.994 percent. The quick rule of three gives a nearby estimate, three divided by n. This is an inference under specific assumptions, rather than certification. It does not cover a different task mix, changed topology, model update or a different tool implementation.
slides.visual: Read the curve as the bound decreasing with more trials. Work through the zero-failure probability in words before naming the formula. Distinguish this one-sided bound from the earlier two-sided Wilson interval.
slides.question: Does zero failures in 300 trials prove zero future failures?
slides.answer: No. Under the stated assumptions it yields a nonzero upper bound, and changes outside that population are untested.
slides.transition: We can design evaluations that make those boundaries visible.

slides.title: Choose tests that can reveal failures
slides.say: A useful test set contains easy and hard tasks, multiple grid sizes, fresh and old inputs, tool errors and both feasible and infeasible cases. Each trial needs a case ID, settings, input snapshot, tool evidence, final status and human corrections. Use an independent reference appropriate to the engineering question. Asking the same model whether its own answer is right does not supply an independent check. Keep final test cases separate from the examples used to tune prompts and adapters. Repeating one prompt many times also leaves task diversity untested. This is a proposed evaluation method. Its value comes from exposing failure types and coverage, rather than producing a single impressive average.
slides.visual: Organize the slide verbally into cases, reference and records. Ask each learner to name one adversarial or difficult condition for their original task.
slides.question: Why hold back a final test set during tuning?
slides.answer: To avoid measuring performance on cases that shaped the system and overstating how well it handles unseen work.
slides.transition: A standard tool interface can help integration, while leaving these tests necessary.

slides.title: MCP connects a workflow to its tools
slides.say: The Model Context Protocol standardizes how an application connects to services exposing tools. The application hosts clients, and each client connects to a server. The server can describe an available operation, accept a request and return a result. In a power workflow, that operation might query a record or call a numerical service. MCP supplies the communication structure. Planning, electrical modeling and validation remain separate responsibilities. The application still checks who is requesting a call, whether the action is allowed, which inputs it uses and what the returned evidence means. An MCP architecture diagram cannot establish numerical accuracy or identify an unreported orchestration library.
slides.visual: Follow host, client and server in the original protocol diagram, then return with the tool result. Give one read-only data call and one simulation call as teaching examples.
slides.question: Who decides whether the returned solver evidence answers the user's question?
slides.answer: The application and its engineering review process must apply the task's checks. The protocol alone cannot decide that.
slides.transition: Documents arriving through those services must also stay within their authority.

slides.title: A retrieved document cannot give itself permission
slides.say: Imagine a retrieved document containing text that tells the assistant to ignore its limits and issue a command. That text is part of the evidence being read. It cannot grant itself operating permission. The application must keep task instructions, user identity and service permissions separate from retrieved content. The trust-boundary diagram shows where the document enters and where an independent action check must apply. Tests should ask whether hostile content changes the case scope, triggers a forbidden call or contaminates the report. Save the blocked request and its reason so the behavior can be inspected. This hostile instruction is an invented classroom example, rather than a reported utility incident.
slides.visual: Trace the retrieved text to the boundary and then to the separate permission check. Ask learners which part of the system can authorize an action.
slides.question: Can a manual or webpage legitimately expand the user's operating permissions?
slides.answer: No. Retrieved content is evidence. Authorization must come from the appropriate user and enforced service policy.
slides.transition: A useful assistant must also improve the complete human task.

slides.title: Measure the whole job, including human review
slides.say: Measure the job from data preparation through agent work, human review and rework. For sequential stages, adding those times gives a useful accounting identity. If work happens in parallel, measure the path that determines completion rather than adding every worker's elapsed time. Include failed attempts, escalations and corrections. A faster draft may still create more reviewer work or miss the operating deadline. Report the spread of times and the difficult cases as well as the average. The conventional monitoring screenshot illustrates the interpretation work an operator does. It is not evidence that the tutorial's timing method was measured in an agent deployment at CAISO.
slides.visual: Point to information the operator must interpret in the real screenshot. Verbally separate machine time, operator attention and total completion time.
slides.question: What should we add to a model response-time benchmark before claiming operator time savings?
slides.answer: Preparation, review, correction, failed attempts and an appropriate comparison on completed tasks.
slides.transition: A pilot can compare that work before authority is expanded.

slides.title: Test whether the assistant helps on comparable tasks
slides.say: Start with shadow mode: save the assistant's proposals while the existing operating process continues to make the decision. Compare comparable tasks with and without assistance. Task difficulty, practice and learning can affect the result, so balance or randomize order where practical. After tuning, retain a fixed final test set. Define stopping rules, error categories and review responsibilities before expanding the pilot. Record disagreements with independent checks and with reviewers. The photograph shows a real training facility, while the comparison design is our teaching proposal. A pilot supports conclusions about the actual tasks, tools, settings and participants tested. Expansion requires evidence for the new scope.
slides.visual: Use the training-facility photo to explain rehearsing a task under controlled conditions. Connect the proposed comparison to the audience task selected at the start.
slides.question: Why can an unbalanced before-and-after comparison exaggerate benefit?
slides.answer: People may have learned the task, conditions may differ or the second set may simply be easier.
slides.transition: Testbeds provide controlled places for that evaluation.

slides.title: Power-sector testbeds provide places to evaluate agents
slides.say: A testbed lets researchers observe a system under selected conditions and deliberately introduce errors or state changes. DOE CESER's July 2026 announcement describes LLNL's Stormbreaker evaluation testbed. EPRI's SAFERai.power develops assessment and risk guidance. These efforts address different roles. The photograph here is ORNL's Grid Operations and Analytics Laboratory, used as power-sector context. It is not a photograph of Stormbreaker. A testbed still needs cases that represent the intended task, and a guidance program does not certify this tutorial's prototype. Use such environments to make failures visible and keep the tested scope explicit.
slides.visual: Identify ORNL as the image source. Name DOE/LLNL and EPRI separately so the photograph does not merge them into a single project.
slides.question: Does access to a testbed prove an agent is ready for deployment?
slides.answer: No. It provides an environment in which relevant performance and failure evidence can be collected.
slides.transition: Our own prototype should face the same standard of evidence.

slides.title: GridGuard: what should this prototype prove?
slides.say: The GridGuard prototype tests proposed actions using OpenDSS on a synthetic feeder. The purpose is to learn whether it improves completed tasks while respecting fixed limits. Save each proposal, its input snapshot, the solver result, rejected alternatives and the reviewer decision. Measure correct feasible proposals, false approvals, modeled limit violations, time and reviewer corrections. The prototype cannot issue live distribution-management commands. Its feeder and results support bounded teaching studies, so we should not present them as a deployed utility control system. A plausible proposal is a starting point. The inspectable evidence and evaluation determine whether it was useful.
slides.visual: Read the feeder as a synthetic model and point to the boundary between proposing and numerical testing. Connect each saved item to one of the three validity checks.
slides.question: What would make a proposal useful to an operator reviewing it?
slides.answer: Clear assumptions, current inputs, relevant numerical evidence, visible failures or limits and a decision within the reviewer's authority.
slides.transition: The next tutorial applies this evidence contract to three cases.

slides.title: Next tutorial: check the proposed action
slides.say: In voltage support, ask whether the proposed action meets the intended model's limits. In restoration, ask what topology and switching assumptions were checked and which load is restored. In cyber response, ask how uncertain or hostile data affect the evidence and permissions. The hands-on tutorial uses one Classroom Labs notebook to explore those questions. It separates fresh numerical calculations from saved Llama episodes. Carry forward our three checks: valid data, valid engineering and a justified decision. The workshop then lets you run, change and inspect the cases directly.
slides.visual: Name the three cases and the evidence question for each. Show the linked hands-on presentation and Classroom Labs entry point without starting a new demonstration here.
slides.question: What should we carry from this session into every lab result?
slides.answer: Its input identity, actual tool evidence, limits, unresolved issues and the human decision boundary.
slides.transition: Close by asking learners to apply the same questions to their own work.

slides.title: Discussion and full sources
slides.say: Return to the task you chose at the beginning. Which paper or workflow is closest to it? Identify one permitted agent action, one tool that would calculate or retrieve the needed evidence and one result an operator would need to review. Then state a failure that should stop or limit the conclusion. Our central lesson is that a credible claim names the task, the test population, its assumptions, observed failures and remaining human work. The source guide links the original papers, utility reports, documentation and figure credits so you can read beyond the slide. Both exercises have worked answers in this script. The follow-on workshop turns this review method into numerical experiments.
slides.visual: Allow one brief audience example and one question. Return to the opening distinction between reported use and measured benefit. Share the source-guide and hands-on links.
slides.question: What evidence would you request before adopting an assistant for your own task?
slides.answer: A bounded assignment, relevant independent tests, inspectable tool records, measured review effort and clear handling of errors and permissions.
slides.transition: Move to the hands-on tutorial or close the session with the full reading guide.
